relationships.description: The stakeholder is the party who imposed, owns, or is affected by the restriction on the solution space, such as the procurement office behind a budget ceiling or the regulator behind a jurisdiction rule.
relationships.evidence: The architecture decision record, policy document, or requirement text stating the constraint names the stakeholder as its originator, approver, or affected party.

relationships.description: The stakeholder has a concern about, or is exposed to, the condition or force that prompts the organization to change, such as compliance officers facing a new regulation.
relationships.evidence: A stakeholder analysis, concern matrix, or driver register lists the stakeholder against the driver as a concerned or affected party.

relationships.description: The stakeholder holds, sponsors, or has a stake in the end state the goal describes, so the goal can be traced back to that party's interests.
relationships.evidence: A strategy document, OKR sheet, or goal register names the stakeholder as the sponsor or owner of the goal.

relationships.description: The stakeholder is the party who cares about, is accountable for, or benefits from reaching the measurable end result.
relationships.evidence: A KPI dashboard, benefits register, or outcome definition lists the stakeholder as owner or beneficiary of the target value.

relationships.description: The stakeholder authored, endorses, or is bound by the normative principle within its scope, such as an architecture board that issued it.
relationships.evidence: The principles catalogue or architecture governance charter records the stakeholder as the principle's owner, approver, or intended audience.

relationships.description: The stakeholder is the party whose need the requirement expresses or who must accept that it has been met.
relationships.evidence: The requirement record (e.g. a Jira story or requirements spec entry) lists the stakeholder in its 'requested by', 'source', or acceptance sign-off field.

relationships.description: The two stakeholders are related parties, for example one group is part of, represents, or shares concerns with the other.
relationships.evidence: An organization chart, RACI matrix, or stakeholder map shows a reporting, membership, or representation link between the two parties.

relationships.description: The stakeholder is the party for whom the stated worth or benefit holds, and from whose perspective the value is expressed.
relationships.evidence: A value proposition canvas, business case, or value statement explicitly names the stakeholder as the recipient of the benefit.

relationships.description: The stakeholder's perspective, input, or priorities shape how a finding about the current state is judged, such as security leads raising the severity of an identified risk.
relationships.evidence: Workshop minutes, review comments, or the assessment report record the stakeholder's input altering or determining the assessment's verdict or rating.

relationships.description: The stakeholder's actions or demands create or intensify the condition prompting change, such as a major customer pressing for a new integration channel.
relationships.evidence: The driver register or strategy rationale cites the stakeholder's demands, complaints, or mandates as the source or amplifier of the driver.

relationships.description: The stakeholder's interests shape the content, priority, or direction of the goal, for example a board steering a goal toward cost reduction.
relationships.evidence: Steering committee minutes, goal-setting records, or revision history show the stakeholder proposing, reprioritizing, or amending the goal.

notes: associated-with and influence to both driver and goal overlap; influence subsumes association when the stakeholder shapes the element, so the associated-with variants risk redundancy unless reserved for passive concern. Stakeholder associated-with constraint is weak; ArchiMate typically links stakeholders to drivers/goals, with constraints reached via requirements.
